clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa7_association_analysis: K-means clustering (k=2-10, 10,000 max iterations, 1000 repetitions) to identify subtypes based on Euclidean distance of deviation maps; Silhouette Index and Calinski-Harabasz Index for optimal cluster selection; one-sample t-tests on deviation values with Bonferroni correction for regional analysis; two-sample t-tests for between-subtype comparisons; Pearson correlation between deviation values and HAMD scores with Bonferroni/FDR correction; partial least squares (PLS) regression to explore spatial correlation between cognitive functions (from Neurosynth) and deviation maps, with bootstrapping (1000 iterations) and permutation tests (10,000 permutations) with spatial-autocorrelation correction; demographic and clinical comparisons using t-tests and chi-square tests
clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa8_key_findings_brief: Two distinct MDD subtypes were identified with opposing patterns of network topology: Subtype 1 showed positive deviations in limbic, frontoparietal, and default mode networks but negative deviations in visual and sensorimotor networks (correlating with higher cognitive functions), while Subtype 2 demonstrated the inverse pattern (correlating with basic perceptual processes).
clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa9_key_findings_detailed: The study identified two distinct neurobiological subtypes of MDD through normative modeling of degree centrality in functional brain networks. Subtype 1 (55% of patients, n=438) exhibited negative deviations in visual (VIS; t=-10.287, corrected p<0.001) and sensorimotor networks (SMN; t=-16.959, corrected p<0.001), but positive deviations in ventral attention (VAN; t=2.433, corrected p=0.018), limbic (LIM; t=9.304, corrected p<0.001), frontoparietal (FPN; t=11.967, corrected p<0.001), and default mode networks (DMN; t=14.590, corrected p<0.001). This pattern suggests overly segregated functional gradients from unimodal to transmodal networks, with cognitive processes weighted toward higher-order functions (memory retrieval, emotion regulation, impulsivity, social cognition). Subtype 2 (45%, n=359) showed the opposite pattern: positive deviations in VIS (t=5.772, corrected p<0.001), SMN (t=16.955, corrected p<0.001), and VAN (t=5.792, corrected p<0.001), but negative deviations in LIM (t=-15.746, corrected p<0.001), FPN (t=-2.422, corrected p=0.019), and DMN (t=-11.550, corrected p<0.001), suggesting overly integrated hierarchical information processing and cognitive emphasis on basic sensory and motor functions. Subtype 2 had significantly higher onset age (t=2.286, p=0.023) and more severe general somatic symptoms (t=2.169, p=0.031) and hypochondriasis (t=2.290, p=0.023) than Subtype 1. In Subtype 2, negative deviations in right posterior inferior temporal gyrus (r=-0.184, corrected p=0.013) and LIM (r=-0.139, corrected p=0.025) were negatively correlated with HAMD scores. Validation using AAL90 atlas showed high consistency (r=0.681-0.823 across networks) with 72.6% clustering overlap. The model showed excellent generalizability in 10-fold cross-validation (SMSE=1.014±0.005, MSLL=0.001±0.004). PLS analysis revealed that cognitive function patterns explained 66.79% and 67.84% of variance in Subtypes 1 and 2, respectively, with significant spatial correlations (r=0.817 and 0.824, both corrected p<0.001).

caa10_key_limitations.answer: Cross-sectional design limits observation of long-term associations and causal relationships; findings not yet validated with external data from different populations; incomplete clinical information (first-episode status, medication usage) for some MDD patients constrains thorough assessment of these clinical factors; cognitive functions analyzed at group level rather than individual level
caa10_key_limitations.supporting_text: while normative models have provided valuable insights into the heterogeneity of MDD and its distinct subtypes by elucidating the age-related alterations of brain function, the reliance on cross-sectional data has limited our capacity to observe longterm associations and establish causal relationships... our findings have not yet been validated with external data from different populations... the incomplete clinical information for certain MDD patients, such as their first-episode status and medication usage, constrained our thorough assessment of these critical clinical factors... this study has significantly advanced our understanding by analyzing cognitive functions at the group level. However, future research could examine the relationship between brain function abnormalities and cognitive functions at the individual level

clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa11_application_notes: The study employed Neurosynth meta-analytic data with 117 cognitive terms from Cognitive Atlas to map cognitive correlates of deviation patterns. K-means clustering with robust evaluation (10,000 max iterations, 1000 repetitions) ensured reliable subtype identification. Sex-stratified analyses and validation with alternative atlas (AAL90) demonstrated robustness. Subtype analyses stratified by medication use and episode status showed no significant differences in deviation patterns (Table S1), suggesting these factors did not confound the subtype classification.

general_note_part.gn1_general_notes: This is a large multi-site study using publicly available REST-meta-MDD data from DIRECT consortium. Two sites (Site 4 and Site 25) were excluded: Site 4 for participant duplication with Site 14, and Site 25 for excessive late-onset depression cases (age>60) and remitted patients. Sites with fewer than 10 MDD or 10 HC were excluded to balance sample size and minimize extreme biases. MDD patients were further excluded if HAMD-17 scores <8. Validation analyses using AAL90 atlas replicated the main findings with high consistency. Age-related increases in degree centrality were observed in left lateral occipital cortex and right frontal orbital cortex, while decreases were seen in left superior temporal gyrus and right temporal pole. The proportion of positive outliers ranged from 0.1255% to 1.6311%, and negative outliers from 0.1255% to 1.2547%. The study data is available at http://rfmri.org/REST-meta-MDD. The network sparsity threshold of 0.05-0.50 at 0.01 intervals was used to avoid biases from single threshold selection. The study used Yeo 7-network parcellation (VIS, SMN, DAN, VAN, LIM, FPN, DMN) for network-level analyses. Each Harvard-Oxford region was assigned to the Yeo network containing the highest number of voxel attributions within that region.
